{{Short description|Concept in topology}}
{{multiple image
| total_width = 320
| image1 = Blue Unknot.png
| image2 = Blue Trefoil Knot.png
| footer = In <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math>, the [[unknot]] is not '''ambient-isotopic''' to the [[trefoil knot]] since one cannot be deformed into the other through a continuous path of homeomorphisms of the ambient space. They are ambient-isotopic in <math>\mathbb{R}^4</math>.

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] subject of [[topology]], an '''ambient isotopy''', also called an ''h-isotopy'', is a kind of [[continuous map|continuous]] distortion of an [[ambient space]], for example a [[manifold]], taking a [[submanifold]] to another submanifold. For example in [[knot theory]], one considers two [[knot (mathematics)|knot]]s the same if one can distort one knot into the other without breaking it. Such a distortion is an example of an ambient isotopy.

More precisely, let <math>N</math> and <math>M</math> be manifolds and <math>g</math> and <math>h</math> be [[embedding]]s of <math>N</math> in <math>M</math>.  A [[continuous map]] 
<math display="block">F:M \times [0,1] \rightarrow M </math> 
is defined to be an ambient isotopy taking <math>g</math> to <math>h</math> if
each <math>F_t: M \rightarrow M, F_t(\cdot) = F(\cdot, t)</math> is a [[homeomorphism]] from <math>M</math> to itself, <math>F_0</math> is the [[identity function|identity map]] and <math>F_1 \circ g = h</math>. This implies that the [[orientation (geometry)|orientation]] must be preserved by ambient isotopies. For example, two knots that are [[mirror image]]s of each other are, in general, not equivalent.
